ch02.note: A shikumen (“stone-framed gate”) is the characteristic Shanghai row house of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries: a two- or three-story brick terrace entered through a stone-arched doorway off a lane. Packed close and easily lost among their neighbors, such lanes gave the underground both cover and quick exits, and recur throughout this book. Corroborated.

ch03.anchor: study at Sun Yat-sen University in Moscow
ch03.note: Sun Yat-sen University in Moscow (KUTK) was founded in 1925 to train Chinese Communist and Kuomintang cadres, and put many of the Party’s leaders of the 1930s through its classes before it closed in 1930. It is distinct from the Communist University of the Toilers of the East, the older and broader Comintern school also named in this book. Corroborated.

ch04.anchor: the Party since the Third Plenary Session of the Eleventh Central Committee
ch04.note: The Third Plenary Session of the Eleventh Central Committee, held in Beijing in December 1978, is the meeting at which Deng Xiaoping’s line prevailed and China turned to “reform and opening.” It became the benchmark from which the Party dated its repudiation of the Cultural Revolution, and thus of the rehabilitations this book records. Corroborated.

ch05.anchor: he threw in with Sun Chuanfang
ch05.note: Sun Chuanfang (1885–1935), a warlord of the Zhili clique, controlled the five provinces of the lower Yangzi—his self-styled “League of Five Provinces”—until the Northern Expedition broke his power in 1926–1927. In 1935 he was shot dead in a Tianjin Buddhist temple by Shi Jianqiao, avenging a father Sun had had executed a decade earlier, in a killing that became a celebrated public cause. Corroborated.

ch10.anchor: the Shanghai Shen Bao and News Daily of April 22
ch10.note: The Shen Bao (申报), founded in 1872, was the largest and most influential Chinese-language daily in Shanghai; its independence gave its pages unusual weight—as the “Wu Hao Notice” affair, late in this book, would turn on. Corroborated.

ch14.anchor: December 1929 to join the China Mutual Aid Society
ch14.note: The China Mutual Aid Society (中国互济会) is the body earlier called the China Relief Society (see the note at chapter 2): the Communist-organized legal-aid and relief society founded in 1925 was reorganized under this name in 1929. Corroborated.

ch14.anchor: a piece of news in Ta Kung Pao
ch14.note: Ta Kung Pao (大公报, “L’Impartial”), founded at Tianjin in 1902, was among the most respected independent Chinese newspapers of the Republican era; it still publishes from Hong Kong and is one of the oldest Chinese-language papers in the world. Corroborated.

ch15.anchor: left Shanghai for the E-Yu-Wan Soviet area
ch15.note: The E-Yu-Wan Soviet—named for the one-syllable classical names of its three provinces, Hubei (E), Henan (Yu), and Anhui (Wan)—straddled the Dabie Mountains and was the second-largest Communist base of the early 1930s and the home of the Fourth Front Army. Under Zhang Guotao its main force was driven out in 1932. Corroborated.

ch16.anchor: he entered the Baoding Army Officers' Academy to study artillery
ch16.note: The Baoding Army Officers’ Academy, in Hebei, was China’s first modern regular-army officer school; in its years of operation (1912–1923) it trained some eleven thousand officers, many of whom became the senior commanders of the warlord and Nationalist armies. With the Yunnan and Whampoa academies it is counted one of the three great cradles of Republican-era officers. Corroborated.

ch17.note: Li Mingrui (1896–1931), a Guangxi general who threw in with the Communists, was commander-in-chief of the Red Seventh and Eighth Armies raised in the Bose and Longzhou uprisings that Deng Xiaoping led in 1929–1930. Captured by Nationalist forces, he was executed in 1931. Corroborated.

ch23.anchor: the State Political Security Bureau in Ruijin
ch23.note: The State Political Security Bureau (Guojia Zhengzhi Baoweiju) was the Chinese Soviet Republic’s political-police and counter-espionage organ, set up at Ruijin in 1931 and modeled on the Soviet Cheka and GPU; its first head, Deng Fa, was nicknamed China’s Dzerzhinsky. It is where the withdrawn Central Special Section men found new work in the Red base. Corroborated.

ch23.anchor: received Snow, Ma Haide, Ding Ling, and others
ch23.note: Ma Haide (George Hatem, 1910–1988), a Lebanese-American physician who reached Shanghai in 1933, was drawn to the Communist cause through Agnes Smedley—the same circle that sheltered Liu Ding—and in 1936 made his way to the Red base, where he took this Chinese name and became the first foreigner admitted to the Chinese Communist Party. He spent the rest of his life in China, notably in the control of leprosy and venereal disease. Corroborated.

ch23.anchor: the day of the Dragon Boat Festival
ch23.note: The Dragon Boat Festival (Duanwu), on the fifth day of the fifth lunar month and later associated with the poet Qu Yuan, is a traditional Chinese holiday; here it simply fixes the date of the travelers’ arrival, in the early summer of 1931. Corroborated.

ch25.note: Shi Liangcai (1880–1934) owned and published the Shen Bao (see the note at chapter 10), making it the most powerful independent voice in the Chinese press. His refusal to bend to the Kuomintang and his paper’s calls to resist Japan cost him his life: on 13 November 1934 Dai Li’s agents ambushed and killed him on the Shanghai–Hangzhou road. Corroborated.

Tao Xingzhi (1891–1946), one of modern China’s foremost educators, studied under John Dewey at Columbia and built a mass-education movement on the maxim “life is education.” A prominent progressive, he advised Shi Liangcai on the reform of the Shen Bao. Corroborated.

ch26.anchor: Shen Anna, sent by Zhou Enlai to penetrate the Kuomintang Central Party Headquarters
ch26.note: Shen Anna (born Shen Wan, 1915–2010) was placed by the Party inside the Kuomintang’s central apparatus as a shorthand stenographer, an assignment Zhou Enlai helped arrange; from the late 1930s to 1949 she transcribed the Nationalists’ highest councils and passed the minutes to the Communists, one of the most productive of the Party’s moles. Corroborated.
